title: What is the true plural of 'fish'?

entries.note: From Greek [[from:Okeanos]], the world-encircling river of early Greek cosmology; Americans tend to say ocean where Brits say [[see:sea]].
A very old Germanic word for any large body of salt or fresh water, which Brits use where Americans often say [[see:ocean]]; related to German [[same-root:See]].
German word that can mean sea, as in Ostsee for the Baltic, or lake; an old Germanic word like English [[same-root:sea]].
An element meaning of the sea or of the open sea, found in the names of the ocean's depth zones, such as the [[see:epipelagic zone]].
The ocean's top layer, whose name literally means upon the surface, from epi- and [[from:pelagic]].
The middle layer of the ocean, its name meaning the middle of the open sea.
A dark layer of the ocean whose name just means deep.
A darker layer of the ocean whose name means bottomless, as can be guessed from [[same-root:abyss]].
Cited to show that the [[same-root:abyssal zone]] means bottomless.
Also called the hadopelagic zone, the deepest layer, named from the same root as [[same-root:Hades]], the underworld.
The underworld, which shares its root with the [[same-root:hadal zone]].
An old Germanic word for big sea creatures, once counted as big fish; originally hw-, like [[see:what]], [[see:where]], [[see:when]] and [[see:who]].
An ancient Indo-European word, cognate with Latin [[same-root:piscis]], once meaning any sea creature; masculine in Old English, so its plural was fishes until relatively recently.
Latin for fish, sharing a distant ancestor with [[same-root:fish]], and the source of [[gave:Pisces]].
From Latin [[from:piscis]]; Jess notes that Old English fiscas looks more like it.
Not a fish to modern eyes; it was named when [[see:fish]] meant any sea creature.
Not a fish; its name invokes the older sense of [[see:fish]] as any sea creature.
The creature is sometimes a big fish and sometimes a [[see:whale]], since whales were once counted as big fish.
A neuter Old English noun with an unchanged plural, the pattern Rob expected [[see:fish]] to follow.
A neuter Old English noun with an unchanged plural, the pattern Rob expected [[see:fish]] to follow.
Literally whale horse; earlier forms such as Old English horse whale were reversed, probably through confusion with a Scandinavian word for the walrus.
The [[see:walrus]]'s binomial: Odobenus means tooth walker and rosmarus comes from Old Norse [[from:hrosshvalr]], horse whale, making it a tooth-walking horse of the sea.
The Old Norse name of the main island of Orkney, now called Mainland or Pomona; it uses the same horse element as [[same-root:hrosshvalr]].
Originally a hw- word, later spelled wh-, like [[see:whale]].
Originally a hw- word, later spelled wh-, like [[see:whale]].
Originally a hw- word, later spelled wh-, like [[see:whale]].
Originally a hw- word, later spelled wh-, like [[see:whale]].
Most likely corpse whale, because its mottled grey body looked like a corpse under the surface; alternatively linked to [[from?:nál]], needle, for its tusk.
The Latin name of the [[see:narwhal]], meaning one tooth one horn; the tusk is a tooth, and what it's used for is debated.
The order of whales, from a Greek word meaning sea monster; [[see:Ceto]] was a primordial Greek sea goddess.
A primordial sea goddess and mother of many monsters in Greek myth, named alongside [[see:Cetacea]].
The division of baleen whales, such as humpbacks.
The toothed whales, which include [[see:dolphin]]s, [[see:porpoise]]s and [[see:sperm whale]]s.
A toothed whale, named from Greek [[from:delphis]], womb, perhaps for giving live birth; unlike a [[see:porpoise]], it has a sickle-shaped fin and cone-shaped teeth.
Originally whale killer, since it hunts baleen whales; also called [[see:orca]], it is both a dolphin and a whale.
Another name for the [[see:killer whale]], from the same root as Tolkien's [[same-root:orc]]s and related to [[same-root:Orcus]], Roman god of the underworld.
The dolphin family, which includes [[see:killer whale]]s and belongs to [[see:Odontoceti]]; [[see:sperm whale]]s are not in it.
Etymologically pig fish, from French [[from:porc]] and [[from:poisson]]; smaller than dolphins, with triangular fins, spade-shaped teeth and ultrasonic calls.
The Old English name for [[see:porpoise]]s, after their rounded snouts and stocky bodies.
From Latin [[from:dorsum]], back, which helps Rob remember where the dorsal fin is.
The animal that [[see:dolphin]] now most commonly refers to.
A river dolphin with a bottlenose shape that is often pink and can turn its neck, which Jess finds creepy.
The binomial of the [[see:orca]]; the genus name Orcinus is related to [[same-root:Orcus]], the Roman god of the underworld.
Long used in English for large deadly sea creatures, from the same root as [[same-root:orca]]; [[see:J. R. R. Tolkien]] drew on its Old English sense of a big, scary thing.
Took his [[see:orc]]s mainly from the word's Old English sense of a big, deadly, scary thing.
The Roman god of the underworld, whose name is related to the genus name in [[same-root:Orcinus orca]].
A former binomial of the [[see:orca]], perhaps for its combative nature or from the same root as [[same-root?:gladiator]], swordsman.
Essentially means swordsman, from the Latin for sword; possibly behind the former name [[see:Orca gladiator]].
A toothed whale in its own family, outside [[see:Delphinidae]], that dives deep for squid and is named after its [[see:spermaceti]]; its clicks outdo a jet engine.
A waxy substance in the [[see:sperm whale]]'s head, prized by whalers, that helps focus sound and buoyancy; the name means sperm of the whale, after its appearance.
Its name is self-explanatory from the bump on its back; its Latin name is [[see:Megaptera novaeangliae]].
Named for looking a bit blue; its Latin name is [[see:Balaenoptera musculus]].
The [[see:blue whale]]'s binomial: Balaenoptera means winged whale, and musculus, related to [[same-root:muscular]], comes from a word meaning mouse.
Related to the musculus, mouse, in [[same-root:Balaenoptera musculus]].
The shellfish; a different spelling of the same word as [[same-root:muscle]], meaning little mouse, perhaps because mussels look like little mice attached to things.
Means little mouse, because a rippling muscle supposedly looks like a mouse crawling underneath; the same word as [[same-root:mussel]].
The [[see:humpback whale]]'s binomial, meaning great winged of New England, after its long fins; its pter element appears in [[same-root:helicopter]] and [[same-root:pterodactyl]].
Contains the same pter, wing, as [[same-root:Megaptera novaeangliae]].
Contains the same pter, wing, as [[same-root:Megaptera novaeangliae]].
Contains the same pter, wing, as [[same-root:Megaptera novaeangliae]].
Origin unknown; it meant scoundrel or swindler from the 1400s and was applied to the fish after [[see:John Hawkins]]'s specimen was exhibited in London in 1569.
The captain whose expedition brought back the specimen that his men called a [[see:shark]], exhibited in London in 1569.
One of the specific older names for sharks, used before [[see:shark]] became the general word.
One of the specific older names for sharks, used before [[see:shark]] became the general word; such sharks are still sometimes called [[see:dogfish]].
What the sharks once called [[see:sea dog]]s are still sometimes called.
The name for hammerheads until the 1740s, before [[see:shark]] became the general word.
A word for [[see:shark]] borrowed from French and Spanish, presumably from encountering sharks in the Caribbean.
Sailors' name for the brown shark, quoted from Melville's Mardi; Rob's favourite, it supports the idea that the [[see:shark]] was named after the human predator.
One of the [[see:shark]]s Melville describes in Mardi, as a dandy with a slender waist and a Bond Street bow.
One of the [[see:shark]]s Melville describes in Mardi, as a portly gourmand with a savage swagger and a collapsed conscience.
One of the [[see:shark]]s Melville describes in Mardi, as a ghost of a fish moving with horrific serenity.
Origin unknown; possibly a sailors' variant of [[from?:squirt]], since squid squirt ink.
From [[from:calamus]], reed or pen, because squid squirt ink and are pen-shaped; unrelated to the calli- of [[unrelated:calligraphy]].
Its calli- means nice, and despite appearances it is unrelated to [[unrelated:calamari]].
Means head foot; Rob is never sure whether the c is hard or soft, just as with [[see:encephalitis]].
Also pronounced with either a hard or a soft c, like [[see:cephalopod]].
Means eight foot and only existed in modern Latin; the plurals octopuses, octopodes and octopi are debated, with octopuses judged most correct.
The ancient Greek word for the [[see:octopus]], pluralised in English as polypi, which Jess cites as precedent for octopi.
Not classical Latin: many binomials never existed in the ancient languages, but were pieced together from classical elements by scientists.
Not a true fish; originally just cuttle, possibly from Germanic words for pocket or scrotum, perhaps related to [[same-root?:cod]]; its genus is [[see:sepia]].
Its [[see:cod]] is not the fish but a word meaning scrotum.
Meaning scrotum in [[see:codpiece]], possibly related to [[same-root?:cuttlefish]]; the fish might be named after it, making it a ball sack of the sea.
The genus of [[see:cuttlefish]], and the brown pigment once made from cuttlefish ink, as in smartphone photo filters.
A swirly-shelled cephalopod whose name means sailor; bestiaries described it sailing with outspread arms, an image perhaps from the [[see:argonaut]]. Jess thinks the ship was named after it.
An octopus whose thin coiled egg case was mistaken for a shell, perhaps the source of early accounts of the [[see:nautilus]].
The shellfish is named after the [[from:barnacle goose]]; the word is probably from French [[from?:bernac]], influenced by [[see?:hibernacule]], or perhaps from bare neck.
Originally just barnacle; a goose said to grow on waterside trees, hanging by its beak from the shell, which then became the [[gave:barnacle]].
Literally means to constrict, clinch or pinch, which is what a clam does; discussed in a previous episode.
Doesn't need the idea of a [[see:clam]] to make sense, since clam itself means to constrict or clinch.
Related to Greek words for bone and shell, such as osteon, and for a potsherd; related to [[same-root:ostracize]], and it gave the name [[gave:Istres]].
From an ancient Greek vote on whom to exile, with names written on pot shards; related to [[same-root:oyster]].
Rob's wife's hometown in southern France, thought to be named after the [[from:oyster]]s off its coast.
A plant-like animal whose name means daughter of the wind, from the Greek for wind, as in [[same-root:anemometer]], which is related to Latin [[same-root:animus]].
From the Greek for nettle, since many sting; the group includes [[see:jellyfish]], [[see:anemone]]s, hydroids and corals.
Another fish that isn't a fish, named from the old sense of [[see:fish]] as any sea creature.
A device for measuring wind, from the same Greek word for wind as [[same-root:anemone]].
Related to the Greek for wind behind [[same-root:anemone]]; it's all about movement.
The group that includes the sea cucumber, meaning spiky or hedgehog skin, from Greek [[from:echinos]], hedgehog; it may link to [[same-root?:echidna]].
The Australasian hedgehog-like animal; Greek echidna meant snake or viper, an odd name for it unless because they eat snakes; possibly linked to [[same-root?:echinoderm]].
So called because a land [[from:urchin]] was a hedgehog; in French it is an [[see:oursin]].
Originally a hedgehog, which gave [[gave:sea urchin]]; calling a Victorian child an urchin likens them to a lost little spiky animal.
French for [[see:sea urchin]]; the same word as [[same-root:hérisson]], hedgehog, taken from a different period in the word's development.
French for hedgehog, spelled with an H; drop the H and it sounds much like [[same-root:oursin]], which is the same word.
A German scientific coinage from a Greek word, used for all sorts of tiny organisms, including eggs, larvae, [[see:diatom]]s and [[see:protozoan]]s.
Not an animal but an alga, often made of two symmetrical halves, that produces 20 to 50% of Earth's oxygen.
Means early animal, from proto-, early, and the Greek for animal found in [[same-root:zoo]] and [[same-root:zodiac]]; includes single-celled organisms like the [[see:amoeba]].
Contains the same Greek word for animal as [[same-root:protozoan]].
Contains the same Greek word for animal as [[same-root:protozoan]].
A single-celled [[see:protozoan]]; Rob settles on the plural amoebas, though Jess suggests adding an e works too.
Simply a Norwegian word for tiny shrimp, one of many fishing words borrowed through contact with Norwegian sailors in the North Sea.
Probably a blend of the [[see:Taino]] word [[from?:baracuta]], solitary person or animal, and a Spanish word meaning overlapping tooth, borrowed via Spanish.
The people living in the Caribbean when the Spanish arrived, whose word baracuta may be behind [[see:barracuda]].
Came to English from Spanish, which got it from Arabic, Latin and ultimately Greek, from a root probably meaning to dart or rush.
Via French from Latin [[from:platessa]], flat, since it's a flatfish; a gift for chip-shop puns like Fred's plaice.
The had- is unknown, but [[see:-ock]] marks something small, so whatever a had was, it was bigger than a haddock.
A suffix implying something small, found in [[see:haddock]], [[see:buttock]], [[see:bullock]] and [[see:hillock]].
An example of the diminutive suffix [[see:-ock]].
An example of the diminutive suffix [[see:-ock]].
An example of the diminutive suffix [[see:-ock]].
Perhaps a diminutive of a word meaning army, because they school, or with [[see:-ing]] meaning the fish associated with the army.
A Germanic suffix that is either diminutive, like [[see:-ling]], or means associated with, as in [[see:Viking]] and [[see:herring]].
A suffix that is more clearly diminutive than [[see:-ing]].
Vik- means bay or camp and [[see:-ing]] means the people of; also discussed in an earlier episode.
Meant spear in Old English, after the fish's long spear-like nose; it's the same gar as in the [[see:Spear-Danes]] of Beowulf's first line.
Named in the first line of Beowulf, using the same Old English word for spear as the fish [[see:gar]].
A tiny herring usually said to be named after [[from?:Sardinia]], but a mention in Aristotle makes that doubtful; the naming might even run the other way.
The island usually said to give its name to [[see:sardine]]s, though the link is uncertain and could run the other way.
Like [[see:sardine]], its relation to [[see:Cyprus]] is murky; discussed in an earlier episode.
The island whose name has a murky relationship with [[see:cypress]] and [[see:copper]].
It's unclear whether it is named after [[from?:Cyprus]] or Cyprus after it.
The Old English word, cognate with Latin [[same-root:anguilla]], little snake; [[see:Aristotle]] thought eels were born from the earth's entrails, and their reproduction long remained mysterious.
A Latin cognate of [[same-root:eel]], meaning snake or little snake.
Described [[see:eel]]s as born from the entrails of the earth.
Not a true [[see:eel]]; three pairs of abdominal organs give it a high-voltage, low-amperage shock used for navigation, communication and stunning prey.
A fish with a fringed head and a large, brightly coloured, scary-toothed mouth; sarcastic here means flesh-tearing, as in [[see:sarcasm]].
To do with the tearing of flesh; being sarcastic is essentially tearing chunks of flesh off someone.
A [[see:carpet shark]] with shaggy lips; the tassels are the shaggy bits, and wobbegong is an Australian Aboriginal word meaning shaggy beard.
So called because their patterns can resemble ornately patterned carpets.
Possibly named for how fast they move; the reef triggerfish's Hawaiian name is [[see:humuhumunukunukuapua'a]].

entries.translation: triggerfish with a snout like a pig
entries.note: The Hawaiian name of the reef [[see:triggerfish]], full of the doubling that Hawaiian uses to intensify meaning.
